chapterNote: The soldier's psalm, the plague psalm, the psalm whispered in hospital rooms and stitched into field jackets. It opens with four names of God in two verses — Most High, Almighty, the LORD, my God — because the shelter is only as strong as the One who casts the shadow. The promises sweep the whole threat-board: the fowler's hidden snare and the open pestilence, terror by night and the arrow by day, the sickness that stalks the dark and the destruction that wastes at noon; a thousand falling on one side and ten thousand on the other while the sheltered man stands. Angels are put under orders for his ways; lion and cobra go under his feet. Satan quoted verses 11 and 12 to Jesus on the temple pinnacle — and cut the quotation exactly where it stopped serving him, for the psalm promises protection in your ways, God's ways, not in stunts demanded of heaven (Matthew 4:6). The psalm's deepest turn is its last: God Himself takes over the speaking, and the promises become first-person — because he clings to Me in love, I will deliver him; he will call, I will answer; I will be WITH him in trouble. Not spared from trouble: accompanied in it, and shown, at the end of long days, His salvation — His yeshuah, whose name is Jesus.

1.text: The one who dwells in the secret place of the Most High will spend his nights under the shadow of the Almighty.
1.amp: He that dwells [yashab] in the secret [sether — hidden] place of the most High [Elyon] shall abide ['lodge', lun, the KJV margin] under the shadow [tsel] of the Almighty [Shaddai].
1.notes: The condition is residence, not visits: yashab (H3427), to dwell, with lun (H3885), to lodge the night through. The sether (H5643) is the hiding place of Psalm 27:5, and the two divine names frame the promise — Elyon (H5945), higher than every threat, Shaddai (H7706), sufficient for every need. His tsel (H6738) is the only shadow that means safety.

2.text: I will say of the LORD, 'He is my refuge, He is my fortress — my God, and in Him I put my trust.'
2.amp: I will say [amar] of the LORD [YHWH], 'He is my refuge [machseh] and my fortress [metsudah]: my God [Elohim]; in Him will I trust [batach].'
2.notes: The creed must be said aloud: amar (H559), spoken ownership. machseh (H4268) is the shelter run to, metsudah (H4686) the crag-fortress held — and four names in two verses (Elyon, Shaddai, YHWH, Elohim) before a single promise is listed: who He is comes before what He does.

3.text: Surely He will tear you free from the fowler's snare and from the pestilence that ruins.
3.amp: Surely He shall deliver [natsal — snatch away] you from the snare [pach] of the fowler [yaqush], and from the noisome [havvah — ruinous] pestilence [deber].
3.notes: Two opposite dangers, one deliverance: the pach (H6341) of the yaqush, the trapper's engineered, hidden, personal snare — and deber, the pestilence, impersonal and airborne. havvah (H1942) is ruin with craving in it: the plague pictured as hungry.

4.text: He will cover you over with His pinions, and under His wings you will take refuge; His faithful truth is your shield and encircling rampart.
4.amp: He shall cover [sakak — screen, hedge in] you with His feathers [ebrah — pinions], and under His wings [kanaph] shall you trust [chasah — take refuge]: His truth [emeth — faithfulness] shall be your shield [tsinnah] and buckler [socherah — surrounding rampart].
4.notes: The mother-bird figure Boaz blessed Ruth with (cf. Ruth 2:12) and Jesus wept over Jerusalem with (cf. Matthew 23:37): kanaph (H3671), the sheltering wing. sakak (H5526) is the hedging-verb of God's protection of Job. And the armor is emeth (H571) — His faithfulness itself as the tsinnah, the full-body shield.

5.text: You will not be afraid of the terror by night, nor of the arrow that flies by day,
5.amp: You shall not be afraid [yare] for the terror [pachad — dread] by night [layil]; nor for the arrow [chets] that flies [uph] by day [yomam];
5.notes: The threat-board's first pair: pachad layil (H6343, H3915), the nameless dread of darkness, and the chets (H2671), the named, aimed danger of daylight. Between them they cover every hour on the clock.

6.text: nor of the pestilence that walks about in the gloom, nor of the destruction that lays waste at high noon.
6.amp: Nor for the pestilence [deber] that walks [halak] in darkness [ophel — thick gloom]; nor for the destruction [qeteb] that wastes [shud] at noonday [tsohorayim].
6.notes: The second pair personifies the killers: deber out halak (H1980), walking its rounds in the ophel (H652), and qeteb (H6986), destruction, working in broad noon light — danger that neither darkness explains nor daylight prevents. The sheltered man is exempted from the fear, not consulted about the hours.

7.text: A thousand may fall at your side, ten thousand at your right hand — to you it will not come near.
7.amp: A thousand [eleph] shall fall [naphal] at your side, and ten thousand [rebabah] at your right hand [yamin]; but it shall not come nigh [nagash] you.
7.notes: Battlefield arithmetic: eleph and rebabah (H505, H7233), casualties on both flanks, and the protected man still standing — not because the danger was small but because nagash (H5066), approach itself, was forbidden it. Providence draws lines plague cannot read but must obey.

8.text: You will only look on with your eyes, and see the wicked receive their wages.
8.amp: Only with your eyes [ayin] shall you behold [nabat] and see [raah] the reward [shillumah — the repayment] of the wicked [rasha].
8.notes: 'Only with the eyes': a spectator's involvement in judgment, no closer. shillumah (H8011) is repayment from the shalam root — the books balanced. What falls on the rasha is wages, not accident (cf. Psalm 37:34).

9.text: Because you have taken the LORD, my own refuge, even the Most High, as your dwelling place,
9.amp: Because you have made [sum — set, appointed] the LORD [YHWH], which is my refuge [machseh], even the most High [Elyon], your habitation [maon — dwelling place];
9.notes: The psalmist hands over his own address: 'my machseh' offered as 'your maon (H4583)' — the dwelling-place word of Psalm 90:1, binding the two psalms together. sum (H7760) is deliberate: shelter is chosen, appointed, moved into.

10.text: no evil will be allowed to befall you, and no plague will come near your tent.
10.amp: There shall no evil [ra] befall [anah] you, neither shall any plague [nega] come nigh [qarav] your dwelling [ohel — your tent].
10.notes: nega (H5061) is the stroke-word of Egypt's plagues, and the ohel (H168) recalls Israel's tents passed over while Egypt's houses wept (cf. Exodus 12:23). The promise is providence's perimeter, and the New Testament reads it in the deepest register: nothing can befall the sheltered man that does not first pass his Father (cf. Romans 8:28).

11.text: For He will give His angels orders concerning you, to guard you in all your ways.
11.amp: For He shall give His angels [malak] charge [tsavah — command] over you, to keep [shamar — guard as watchmen] you in all your ways [derek].
11.notes: tsavah (H6680): angels under written orders, with shamar (H8104) as the duty and 'all your derek (H1870)' as the jurisdiction — your ways, the paths of obedience, which is precisely the clause Satan omitted on the pinnacle (cf. Matthew 4:6; Luke 4:10). Protection covers the road God gave, not the leap He never asked for.

12.text: In their hands they will lift you up, so that you do not so much as strike your foot against a stone.
12.amp: They shall bear you up [nasa] in their hands [kaph — palms], lest you dash [nagaph] your foot [regel] against a stone [even].
12.notes: nasa (H5375) in the kaph (H3709), the open palms: angelic care measured down to the stubbed toe — the guarding of verse 11 applied at pebble scale. Grace runs both magnitudes at once: armies fall at your side, and your regel is watched on the gravel.

13.text: You will tread on the lion and the cobra; the young lion and the serpent you will trample underfoot.
13.amp: You shall tread [darak] upon the lion [shachal] and adder ['asp', pethen, the KJV margin]: the young lion [kephir] and the dragon [tannin — the serpent, the monster] shall you trample [ramas] under feet.
13.notes: From protection to dominion: darak and ramas (H1869, H7429), treading and trampling. The menagerie is deliberate — shachal and kephir, open violence; pethen and tannin (H8577), venomous cunning and the old chaos-serpent itself. The seed crushing the serpent underfoot is Eden's oldest promise (cf. Genesis 3:15; Romans 16:20).

14.text: 'Because he has bound himself to Me in love, therefore I will deliver him; I will set him up out of reach, because he has known My name.
14.amp: 'Because he has set his love [chashaq — attached himself in desire, clung in love] upon Me, therefore will I deliver [palat] him: I will set him on high [sagab — lift beyond reach], because he has known [yada] My name [shem].
14.notes: God Himself takes the microphone for the finale, and the ground of it all is disclosed: chashaq (H2836), the clinging love-word used of a bridegroom (cf. Deuteronomy 7:7, of God's own love for Israel). sagab (H7682) sets the lover where nothing reaches, and yada shem — knowing the Name — is covenant intimacy, not information.

15.text: He will call on Me, and I will answer him; I Myself will be with him in trouble; I will rescue him and load him with honor.
15.amp: He shall call [qara] upon Me, and I will answer [anah] him: I will be with him in trouble [tsarah]; I will deliver [chalats — draw him out], and honour [kabad — make weighty with glory] him.
15.notes: The promise beneath all the promises: not exemption from tsarah (H6869) but company inside it — 'I will be WITH him', the Immanuel-clause (cf. Isaiah 43:2; Daniel 3:25). chalats (H2502) draws him out the far side, and kabad (H3513) is honor with weight: the rescued man ends up glorified, not merely intact.

16.text: With length of days I will satisfy him, and I will show him My salvation.'
16.amp: With long life ['length of days', orek yom, the KJV margin] will I satisfy [saba] him, and show [raah] him My salvation [yeshuah].'
16.notes: saba (H7646): not merely long days but days that satisfy — quantity with contentment in it. And the last word is yeshuati, 'My yeshuah (H3444)' — the salvation-name that Hebrew ears would one day hear spoken as Yeshua: the psalm's final promise is to SEE His salvation, and Simeon, holding the infant Christ, announced it fulfilled (cf. Luke 2:30).
